title: Julia Set
body:
Same iteration as the [[Mandelbrot Set]], $z_{n+1} = z_n^2 + c$, with the two roles swapped:

| | Varies over the plane | Held fixed |
|---|---|---|
| [[Mandelbrot Set]] | $c$, one point per pixel | $z_0 = 0$ |
| Julia set | $z_0$, one point per pixel | $c$, chosen once |

So there is **one** Mandelbrot set and **a different Julia set for every $c$**. The filled Julia set
$K_c$ is the set of starting points whose orbits stay bounded under that fixed $c$; the Julia set
proper is its boundary. The same escape criterion and the same iterate-until-bored algorithm apply,
with the same one-sided answer.

The relationship between the two is the good part, and it is why the Mandelbrot set is worth
plotting at all:

> **$c$ lies in the Mandelbrot set exactly when the Julia set for that $c$ is connected.**

Outside, the Julia set shatters into a totally disconnected dust (Fatou dust). So the Mandelbrot set
is a *catalogue*: an index of every Julia set, laid out so that its position tells you the shape of
the corresponding one. Picking $c$ from near the boundary gives the intricate Julia sets, from deep
inside gives smooth deformed circles, and from outside gives dust.

See [[Complex Convergence]] for what bounded means here, and [[Complex Numbers]] for the squaring.
